production.title: Amazon Just Gave Its Tablets the Apps Fire Tablet Owners Wanted

narration:
A cheap tablet was never really cheap if it couldn't run your apps.
And for years, that was the deal with Amazon's Fire tablets,
like a TV that only picked up a handful of channels
while everyone else had the full list.
This month, Amazon finally switched on the rest.
Over the next few minutes, we'll see why the old tablets felt limited,
what made Amazon change, what you gain, and how to decide before you buy.
So start with what was going on inside the old Fire tablets.
Back then, they ran Fire OS, Amazon's own version of Android,
and Android is simply what lets apps run on most tablets and phones.
But instead of Google's app store, Amazon gave you its own,
which meant fewer apps, and some that arrived late or not at all.
So if your bank, your school or your favourite streaming app was missing,
you either went without it or used a workaround,
meaning a riskier, unofficial way of installing it yourself.
And developers felt it too, with an extra version to build and fix.
In other words, you saved money and paid for it in missing channels.
Which raises a fair question, why give up a setup that kept prices low?
Because people don't buy a tablet for itself, they buy it for the apps.
On October eighth, twenty twenty-six, Amazon announced three new tablets,
the Alexa Tablet 8, the Tablet 11, and the Tablet 12 Pro,
and all three run Android with Google Play built in.
Google Play is Google's full app store, the whole channel list,
which puts these tablets on equal footing with any other Android tablet.
Amazon is also aiming higher, with aluminum bodies and Alexa Plus,
its newer, smarter assistant, so these aren't just old tablets with new names.
Now bring that into an ordinary day.
Say your family already uses YouTube, Netflix, Gmail and Google Docs.
With Google Play there, each one is a normal download,
which means a student can open class documents straight away,
instead of hunting for a substitute and learning new menus.
A parent gets the same streaming service the family already pays for,
and nobody has to rebuild their routine from scratch.
Still, more channels don't make every programme good,
because some Android apps are built for phones and look stretched on a tablet.
The real win is choice without technical workarounds.
And that's where it can go wrong for your wallet,
because the full list costs more.
The Alexa Tablet 8 starts at two hundred twenty-nine ninety-nine,
the Tablet 11 at three hundred twenty-nine ninety-nine,
and the Tablet 12 Pro at four hundred ninety-nine ninety-nine.
By comparison, the recent Fire HD 10 topped out
around one hundred eighty dollars before discounts.
That's why a little homework before you pay is worth it, in four steps.
First, write down the three apps you open every single day.
Second, search for each one in Google Play and check it supports tablets.
Third, compare the new price with an older Fire tablet plus workarounds.
Finally, ask whether you'd really use Alexa Plus, or just pay for it.
Remember this, Amazon traded some low price for the full channel list.
Your three apps tell you whether those extra channels are worth it to you.
And if this helped, follow the channel,
because every week we break down tech decisions like this one.
Which brings us back to that old TV,
would you pay more for all the channels?

research.summary:
Original explainer draft: Amazon’s big tablet change is not just a new name—it is a change in the software bargain. On October 8, 2026, Amazon announced three Alexa Tablets running Android with built-in Google Play access. That means buyers can download familiar apps such as YouTube, Netflix, Gmail and Google Docs without relying on Amazon’s smaller app catalog. ([aboutamazon.com](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/new-amazon-alexa-tablets-alexa-plus))

The old Fire-tablet experience was more limited. Fire OS was an Android-based fork, but Amazon supplied its own app store instead of Google Play. In plain language: Android was the underlying language, but Amazon controlled the store where users went to get apps. If an app was missing, outdated or poorly supported there, installing it could require workarounds—or simply was not practical for an ordinary buyer. Reuters reported that consumers and developers had complained about those limitations, including the need for developers to maintain another version of their apps. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/amazon-launches-first-android-tablets-raising-prices-and-incorporating-alexa-4939121))

So why make the switch? The move gives Amazon a better chance of being considered a normal Android-tablet maker rather than a low-cost device with a restricted app ecosystem. It also supports Amazon’s attempt to move upmarket: the new tablets use aluminum designs and include more capable hardware, while Alexa+ becomes a central feature. ([investing.com](https://www.investing.com/news/stock-market-news/amazon-launches-first-android-tablets-raising-prices-and-incorporating-alexa-4939121))

The trade-off is price. The new Alexa Tablet 8 starts at $229.99, the Tablet 11 at $329.99 and the Tablet 12 Pro at $499.99. Amazon’s previous Fire HD 10 line topped out around $180 before discounts, according to Reuters. Wider app access makes the new tablets more useful, but it also removes some of the old Fire line’s strongest appeal: being extremely cheap. ([aboutamazon.com](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/new-amazon-alexa-tablets-alexa-plus))

There is one remaining caveat: access to Google Play means more apps, not necessarily that every Android app is perfectly designed for a large screen. The real question is whether familiar apps plus Amazon’s hardware and Alexa features are worth paying more for. ([arstechnica.com](https://arstechnica.com/gadgets/2026/10/amazons-new-alexa-tablets-drop-the-fire-branding-but-are-more-android-than-ever/))

Would you buy an Amazon tablet now that it has the apps you already use?

metadata.title: Amazon Alexa Tablets Get Google Play: Are They Worth It?
metadata.description:
Amazon is replacing its budget-focused Fire tablet approach with the new Alexa Tablet 8, Alexa Tablet 11, and Alexa Tablet 12 Pro. All three run Android with Google Play built in, giving users access to apps that were often missing or difficult to install on older Fire tablets. ([aboutamazon.com](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/new-amazon-alexa-tablets-alexa-plus?utm_source=openai))

This video explains what changed, why the new tablets cost more, and whether Google Play, Alexa Plus, and the upgraded hardware make them worth buying. We also compare the prices with older Fire tablets and share a simple checklist to use before choosing one. ([aboutamazon.com](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/new-amazon-alexa-tablets-alexa-plus?utm_source=openai))
